name: Qatar
governanceModel: State-led strategy and sectoral guidance, with a phased path toward formal AI regulation still underway

overview:
Qatar has pursued AI policy primarily through strategy and sectoral guidance rather than a single binding AI law. Its 2019 National AI Strategy set out six pillars — education, data access, employment, business, research and ethics — and a 2021 Cabinet Decision (No. 10 of 2021) established an inter-ministerial Artificial Intelligence Committee, coordinated through the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), to implement it. Since then, the National Cyber Security Agency (NCSA) issued 'Guidelines for Secure Usage and Adoption of AI' (February 2024), and 2025 saw the publication of 'Principles and Guidelines for Ethical Use of AI.' Reporting describes a phased approach — foundation-building (2024-2025), sectoral implementation (2025-2026) and full deployment with GCC-wide alignment (2026-2027) — with formal, binding AI regulation reportedly still expected only in 2026 or 2027. One concrete, narrower step arrived in January 2026, when the Qatar International Court and Dispute Resolution Centre (QICDRC) issued a Procedural Directive governing AI use in litigation, among the first formal legal controls on AI deployment in the country.

Qatar's more visible recent AI activity has been in infrastructure and capital deployment rather than rulemaking. In December 2025, Qai — a state-backed AI infrastructure company under the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) — and Brookfield Asset Management announced a $20 billion joint venture to build AI data-center and compute infrastructure in Qatar and internationally, positioning Qatar alongside Saudi Arabia's Humain and the UAE's G42 as a third major Gulf player in the AI infrastructure race. Ooredoo, via its data-center spinoff Syntys, has separately launched a sovereign AI cloud built on Nvidia GPUs. This buildout has drawn scrutiny from regional analysts over the water and energy demands of data centers in one of the world's most water-stressed countries, an area where Gulf-wide regulatory standards remain largely undeveloped.

atAGlance.regulatoryApproach: Phased, strategy-led approach built on the 2019 National AI Strategy and 2021 AI Committee, with sector-specific guidance (cybersecurity, ethics, judicial AI use) rather than a single binding AI law so far

atAGlance.governmentInvolvement: High — the state, via QIA-backed Qai and MCIT-led strategy, is a direct investor and coordinator in AI infrastructure and policy rather than solely a regulator
atAGlance.industrialStrategy: Large-scale sovereign AI compute buildout via the Qai-Brookfield joint venture and Ooredoo/Syntys's Nvidia-powered sovereign AI cloud, framed as part of the Qatar Digital Agenda 2030

currentDirection.summary: Qatar's recent trajectory has been dominated by rapid capital deployment into AI infrastructure — most visibly the $20B Qai-Brookfield joint venture announced in December 2025 — rather than new binding rules. On the regulatory side, movement has been narrow and procedural (the QICDRC's January 2026 directive on AI in litigation) rather than comprehensive; officials have signaled that fuller sectoral and GCC-aligned AI regulation is not expected until 2026-2027, so the near-term emphasis remains on strategy, infrastructure and ethics guidance rather than enforceable AI-specific law.

recentDevelopments.text: The GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) steering committee is reported to have announced a common regional AI policy — shared principles on AI ethics, data privacy, security and cross-border cooperation among member states — as a step toward a unified Gulf AI strategy. This aligns with Qatar's own phased plan, which explicitly anticipates GCC-wide alignment by 2026-2027, though details on scope, timeline and enforcement remain thin in early reporting.

Qai (Qatar's state AI company, a subsidiary of the Qatar Investment Authority) and Brookfield Asset Management announce a $20B strategic partnership to build AI data-center and compute infrastructure in Qatar and international markets.

Hyperscaler and local data-centre capacity expands to support Qatar's AI push: Microsoft's Azure region in Qatar is reported to be growing, Google Cloud's Doha region is operational, and local operator MEEZA is expanding AI and data-centre capacity backed by a roughly $200M funding facility — reinforcing infrastructure as the country's most active AI thread ahead of comprehensive regulation.

Qatar International Court and Dispute Resolution Centre (QICDRC) issues Procedural Directive No. (1) of 2026, formally regulating the use of AI tools in litigation before the Court, including mandatory disclosure and verification of AI-generated content.
Ooredoo launches a sovereign AI cloud in Qatar built on Nvidia Hopper GPUs, operated through its data-center spinoff Syntys.

imec, a leading international nanotechnology R&D institute, announces a new regional research and development hub at Qatar Science and Technology Park in Doha, focused on AI-enhanced chip design, advanced computing and sustainable innovation.
Jahez Group (Saudi Arabia) completes acquisition of a 76.56% stake in Qatar's Snoonu, marking what local commentary described as Qatar's first unicorn-level tech exit.

policyAndRegulation.title: QICDRC Procedural Directive No. (1) of 2026 on AI in Litigation
policyAndRegulation.summary: Regulates use of AI tools by litigants and legal representatives before the Qatar International Court and Dispute Resolution Centre, requiring verification and disclosure of AI-generated legal content.

researchEcosystem.summary: Qatar's AI research is concentrated at the Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI), part of Hamad Bin Khalifa University and Qatar Foundation, which runs a dedicated Qatar Center for Artificial Intelligence (QCAI) focused on Arabic-language NLP, speech technology, social computing and responsible AI, and partners with Boeing on applied research. US branch campuses in Education City — Carnegie Mellon University in Qatar and Texas A&M University at Qatar — also conduct AI-related research funded substantially through the Qatar National Research Fund (QNRF), though US reporting in 2026 has raised questions about the scale and transparency of Qatari funding to Carnegie Mellon's home campus, a dynamic that sits alongside (but is distinct from) the Doha campus's own AI research output.

notableGaps.note: Qatar has strategy documents, ethics principles and sector-specific guidance, but no single binding, cross-sector AI statute; officials have signaled formal regulation is expected only in 2026-2027.

No Gulf-wide or Qatar-specific mandatory framework on water-use effectiveness or heat-adapted data-center design has been identified, despite Qatar's status as one of the most water-stressed countries globally.
AI policy coordination runs through an inter-ministerial Committee under MCIT rather than a standalone AI regulatory authority.

debates.topic: Qatar's compute-diplomacy bet: sovereignty ambitions versus dependence on foreign capital and hyperscalers
debates.summary: Qatar's entry into the Gulf AI infrastructure race — via the $20B Qai-Brookfield joint venture and Ooredoo's Nvidia-powered sovereign cloud — is framed by officials as building 'sovereign' AI capacity, but relies heavily on foreign capital, foreign chip supply and international partners.
debates.expanded: Regional analysts have noted that Qatar's move mirrors similar bets by Saudi Arabia (via Humain) and the UAE (via G42), all of which pair large domestic ambitions with deep reliance on US and international capital, hardware and cloud partners. Whether this produces durable, independent Qatari AI capability — as opposed to hosting infrastructure largely owned or financed by outside investors and dependent on Nvidia GPU supply — remains an open and largely unresolved question in available commentary, and Qatar's own AI research and model-development base (concentrated mainly at QCRI) remains modest relative to the scale of the announced infrastructure investment.

debates.topic: Water and energy strain from Gulf AI data-center buildout in a highly water-stressed country
debates.summary: Regional policy analysts have raised concerns that large-scale AI data-center expansion, including Qatar's, is proceeding faster than water- and energy-specific regulatory standards, in a country that ranks among the world's most water-stressed.
debates.expanded: Cooling data centers in the Gulf's hot, humid climate is water-intensive, and freshwater in the region depends heavily on energy-intensive desalination; one estimate cited by regional researchers projects Gulf data centers could consume over 426 billion liters of water annually by 2030. Analysts note there is no GCC-wide framework mandating water-use-effectiveness limits or climate-adapted data-center design, meaning Qatar's data-center buildout (including the Qai-Brookfield venture) is proceeding without binding sustainability guardrails specific to this risk, even as broader ethical-AI guidance has been published.
